faq.q: What helps when I feel worried?
faq.a: Slow belly breaths, telling someone your worry, and checking the facts all help. Writing the worry down can make it feel smaller.
asks: How do I calm a worry?

faq.q: What helps when I feel sad?
faq.a: Talking to someone you trust, a hug, drawing or writing about it, or doing something cosy can help. It is okay to cry too.
asks: How do I feel better when I am sad?

faq.q: What helps when I feel angry?
faq.a: Stop, take slow breaths, and move your body, like jumping or walking. When you are calmer, use words to say what is wrong.
asks: How do I calm down when I am angry?

faq.a: It is different for everyone. Try each tool when you are calm, notice which ones help you most, and keep those as your favourites.
asks: What is the best way to calm down?

faq.q: What if none of my feelings tools work?
faq.a: That happens sometimes, and it is okay to need more help. Talk to a trusted grown-up, a school counsellor or a doctor, who can help you find what works.

facts: The Zones of Regulation, a programme created by occupational therapist Leah Kuypers in 2011, uses four colours to help children notice and manage their feelings.
Calming tools work best when you practise them while calm, so they are easy to use when a big feeling arrives.

quiz.show: Which tool can help cool down anger?
quiz.why: Moving uses up the hot, angry energy in your muscles safely.

wrong.0: Shouting at someone usually makes things worse.
wrong.1: Breaking things can hurt you and others.

quiz.say: When is the best time to practise your feelings tools?
quiz.show: When is the best time to practise your feelings tools?
quiz.why: Practising when calm makes the tools easy to remember when big feelings come.

wrong.0: Like any skill, feelings tools get better with practice.
wrong.2: It is very hard to learn a new tool in the middle of a big feeling.
